doc.title: Jim Hall — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Django Reinhardt and meeting his son Babik
summary: Hall talks about Django's injured hand, the Nazi years, a book on Reinhardt and meeting Babik at a festival.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: The other person that I think was an early influence on you might have been Django Reinhardt.
Do you have any thoughts about what you tuned into there?

Yeah, in a certain sense, the exact opposite of Charlie Christian, ‘cause he played flurries of notes, which was remarkable because, as you know, his hand had been seriously injured in a fire ‘cause he grew up in a, I was gonna say a gypsy household, a gypsy camp, or something. And, and during the war to end all wars… how’s that for World War II? That didn’t work too well, did it? He just kinda disappeared from view. I though maybe he had died, and he was still alive in France. And that was fascinating
that, that he could basically (unintelligible), he could basically just use these two fingers, and occasionally he could use these guys, but then he’d have to push them up with his other hand so…
Yeah, he was… It’s quite a, quite an inspiration. Did you send me that book on Reinhardt?

Yeah. Well, that was fascinating because whoever wrote the book about Django Reinhardt had done tons of research, and what I had forgotten was that the Nazis treated Gypsies just about as badly as they treated Jewish people. And it was fascinating how Reinhardt dealt with that. He must have been a great character. He would park his car with his family in it, and (sounds like “some Mary”) and his Nazi troops would come over and start giving them a bad time, and he’d make up some kind of story or something. I think I mentioned I got to meet his son, Babik, one time.

There was a… there was a Reinhardt festival at that river in France — I forget the name of it. And Babik played right before Larry Goldings and me. And, but Django was known… I think he used an amplifier just right at the end of his life, but he was known for acoustic guitar. And Babik had these huge amplifiers. He said, “I’m goin’ another direction. To hell with that,” you know. (laughs) Cracked me up. But he seemed very nice. He had, he had heard a tune called (Beja Flor?), a Brazilian tune that I recorded, and he didn’t speak English very well, but he just said it, he was raving about that. So that was… Again, the camaraderie among musicians is great so…
